name: Data Integrity
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Knowing Nothing Was Changed Along the Way
lesson.summary: Data integrity is the assurance that information has not been altered, accidentally or deliberately, since it was created, and hash functions turn that assurance into something you can actually check.
lesson.body:
Trust, in its most general sense, is a bet you make that something will behave the way you expect even though you cannot personally verify every detail of it. Data integrity narrows that bet down to one specific question: has this piece of data been changed since I last knew its state, whether by a transmission error, a hardware fault, or someone deliberately tampering with it? Without a way to answer that question, trusting any data you did not personally and continuously observe would require trusting every system and every person it passed through, which does not scale past a very small circle.

Hash functions turn that abstract worry into a concrete, checkable fact. If you compute a hash of a file at the moment you create it and record that hash somewhere safe, you can later recompute the hash of the file as it exists now and compare the two values. If they match, the file is, with extremely high confidence, unchanged. If they differ, even by a single flipped bit, the hashes will look completely different, and you know immediately that something happened to the data between then and now. This is a much narrower and more mechanical claim than "I trust this data" in the everyday sense; it says nothing about who produced the data or whether its original content was true, only that whatever content it started with has not been silently altered since.

A familiar example is downloading software. Many projects publish a SHA-256 checksum alongside an installer file. After downloading, a cautious user can hash the file locally and compare it to the published value. If the download was corrupted, or if an attacker on the network intercepted the file and swapped in a modified version, the checksum will not match, and the mismatch is the warning. This only works, though, if the published checksum itself was obtained through a channel the user trusts, which is a reminder that integrity checks push the trust problem back one step rather than eliminating it entirely; someone still has to vouch for the original hash.

Blockchains apply this same idea structurally rather than as an optional extra step. Each block contains the cryptographic hash of the block before it, so the blocks form a chain where altering any historical block changes its hash, which breaks the reference stored in the next block, which changes that block's hash, and so on all the way to the most recent block. Rewriting history without every honest participant noticing would require redoing that chain of hashes faster than the rest of the network extends it, which is what makes blockchain data structurally tamper-evident rather than merely tamper-resistant. It is worth being precise, though, that integrity alone does not tell you who wrote the data or whether it was honest in the first place; those questions belong to authentication and non-repudiation, covered next.
